items.title: At Least 68 Killed in Train Crash in Spain, Officials Say
items.summary: A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another near Toledo, months after a crash involving the same carriers killed dozens and stunned the country.
items.full_text: Oct. 28, 2026, 1:08 p.m. ET The leader of Spain’s conservative opposition party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded “answers” and urged the national government on Wednesday to conduct an independent review of the entire railway network. “Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure, what condition the tracks and safety systems are in, what warnings were received from Adamuz and what measures were taken,” he said, referring to the fatal January train crash near the city of Adamuz and what lessons, if any, the authorities had learned from it. Oct. 28, 2026, 1:01 p.m. ET The U.S. State Department said in a statement that several U.S. citizens were among those injured in the crash. It did not provide information about their conditions. Oct. 28, 2026, 12:00 p.m. ET José Bautista Reporting from the scene When the crash happened, Yahadi Mohamed Maulud, 41, who lives in the nearby town of Yébenes, loaded his car with water bottles and rushed to help. “We found a massacre,” he said, describing torn limbs and a blood-covered woman searching for her brother. One of the first to arrive at the scene, he helped to move injured passengers and carry stretchers. Maulud said he often took the train himself to Madrid for business, but no more. “I’m never getting on that train again.” Oct. 28, 2026, 11:45 a.m. ET So many people showed up at Madrid hospitals on Wednesday to donate blood for victims of the train crash that the authorities are asking citizens to wait until Thursday or the following days, when more donations will be needed. “The response from the people of Madrid to the call for blood donations is overwhelming,” said Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid’s regional president. “Thank you, everyone.” Oct. 28, 2026, 11:03 a.m. ET Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon. “It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while today’s accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” Spain needs to understand “what is the origin of this tragedy,” he said. Sánchez offered his condolences to the families of victims and thanked emergency workers. He also declared three days of official mourning, as he did after the January crash. Credit... Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Oct. 28, 2026, 10:52 a.m. ET Emiliano García-Page, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, said the death toll from the crash had risen to 68. Twenty-four of those killed were on the Renfe train and the others were on the Iryo train, he said. “Firefighters, with the help of cranes, are still working to determine whether there are more fatalities,” he said, “possibly beneath some of the carriages or among the twisted wreckage they have become.” Oct. 28, 2026, 10:01 a.m. ET José Bautista Reporting from the scene In the middle of fields of alfalfa and almond trees, a seemingly endless procession of ambulances, police cars and firetrucks drove in and out of the crash scene, as rescue helicopters flew low overhead. The trains seemed twisted together, a mass of mangled metal. Dozens of Civil Guard officers, some wearing the white protective suits used by forensic investigators, were inspecting the scene and gathering evidence. Broken cables and fallen utility poles were scattered all around. A group of Catholic priests walked out from the area where the trains were located. “We came to pray for the dead,” said the Rev. Luis Lucendo, 63, a vicar of Toledo and parish priest in Villacañas, a nearby town. “One man told us that his wife had died, and I was able to make the sign of the cross over her,” Father Lucendo said. “They were going to spend the day in Córdoba, but this is where their journey ended.” Credit... Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Oct. 28, 2026, 9:37 a.m. ET At least 64 people were killed in the train crash, the emergency services of Castilla-La Mancha said on Wednesday afternoon. The toll makes the accident one of the deadliest in the country’s history. Credit... Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Oct. 28, 2026, 9:26 a.m. ET Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is traveling to Urda to offer support to first responders and express his support to the families of victims, his government said. Oct. 28, 2026, 8:35 a.m. ET The president of Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed that at least 30 people had been killed in the train crash, a number that may rise. About 80 people were injured, 50 of them, according to García-Page, with severe injuries. Oct. 28, 2026, 7:53 a.m. ET Blood donation groups in the area of the train crash are urging donors to come to hospitals in Toledo and Ciudad Real to “urgently replenish the reserves. Blood of all types will be needed.” Oct. 28, 2026, 7:32 a.m. ET Videos shot by passengers after the crash show parts of the derailed carriages pulverized, with charred wheels, and bags and seats strewn across an embankment. Emergency workers tend to the injured or hover over people covered in Mylar blankets. The arid field outside the small towns of Los Yébenes and Urda has become a parking lot of emergency vehicles and tents. Credit... Manu Fernandez/Associated Press Oct. 28, 2026, 7:24 a.m. ET Video filmed inside one of the trains and verified by The New York Times shows smoke rising from a charred, mangled carriage on the slope of the rail line. The footage was first shared by the Spanish radio station Capital Radio, which said an employee had been on one of the trains at the time of the crash. Video Credit Credit... Capital Radio, via Agence France-Presse Oct. 28, 2026, 6:37 a.m. ET The first eyewitness reports from the crash are beginning to trickle in on Spanish media. Passengers are describing an awful impact that tossed people from the dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. Passengers crawled out of windows and lay in in a nearby field, where local workers, who heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies. Credit... Javier Soriano/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Oct. 28, 2026, 6:27 a.m. ET The crash comes months after a deadly collision in January in southern Spain that involved the same carriers. That accident, in which two high-speed trains collided, killing 46 people, was the country’s worst railway disaster since 2013. An official report on what caused the January crash is not yet available, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause. Oct. 28, 2026, 6:22 a.m. ET Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement that it was deploying a military emergency unit and Civil Guard officers to the scene of the crash in the province of Toledo. Investigators from Spain’s Major Disaster Unit are also en route.

items.title: Rivals in Israel Election Strike Tone of Triumph, but Outcome Is Far From Clear
items.summary: Addressing supporters after midnight, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, who leads a bloc of opposition parties, both expressed confidence that they will lead Israel’s next government. Vote counting could take days.
items.full_text: Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war. The exit polls, if accurate, suggest that neither Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc nor the one led by Mr. Eisenkot , a former military chief whose son was killed in the Gaza war, will be able to form a government without relying on two Arab parties that were projected to win as many as 17 or 18 seats in Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu effectively ruled out including them in a governing coalition, and Mr. Eisenkot and his partners have balked at the idea, too. One option analysts are already weighing is whether Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most far-right government in Israeli history, could join with Mr. Eisenkot or others in the opposition to form a unity government. But a unity government would face major obstacles, given how deeply Mr. Eisenkot’s voters despise Mr. Netanyahu, and because the two would have to agree on which of them would serve as prime minister. Mr. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, while Mr. Eisenkot has called the prime minister unfit to lead Israel. Much remained unclear early Wednesday morning in Israel. Making matters even murkier, Israel’s exit polls have a spotty history of accuracy, particularly in tight races. Mr. Eisenkot appeared onstage past midnight at his post-election party and attempted to strike a tone of triumph — as well as defiance toward Mr. Netanyahu. “Tonight we got the answer: The public wants change,” he said. Mr. Netanyahu addressed his supporters a few hours later, invoking his relationship with President Trump and repeating his pre-election talking points about removing the threat of Iran. He sounded triumphant, saying it was clear that Likud had emerged as the largest party in Israel and mocking months of pre-election polls that showed his party trailing behind that of Mr. Eisenkot. “We must form a strong right-wing government,” he declared. In the coming days, after official vote totals are released and parliamentary seats are allocated to parties, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will invite the party leader he thinks has the best chance to assemble a governing coalition. Such a coalition would usually have to be made up of at least 61 lawmakers, though Mr. Eisenkot has floated the idea of forming a minority government. One factor not reflected in exit polls are the hundreds of thousands of votes cast by Israelis at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In the previous election, those votes tended to favor the coalition of Mr. Netanyahu and his allies. Here’s what else to know: Arab parties: The exit polls pointed to at least one surprise in projecting that two Arab parties would win as many as 17 or 18 seats in the 120-seat Parliament. That would be their strongest showing ever, and potentially give them an important role in forming the next government. Read more › War fears: Amid reports that Mr. Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Mr. Eisenkot warned him in his speech to supporters not to abuse his power as caretaker prime minister to influence the process of forming a new government. “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” he said. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, told a television interviewer that the turnout showed that Arab voters, who make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, had channeled their “frustration and despair” into “hope.” He said he wanted to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way” and that his first priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” that achieved that goal. The Arab parties’ strong showing may make them kingmakers. But building a governing coalition with Arab participation remains a fraught exercise in Israel. Many Israeli Jews believe that a parliamentary majority should not rely on the support of Arab lawmakers. People waiting to cast ballots in Umm al-Fahm, one of the largest Arab towns in Israel, on Tuesday. Credit... Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Most Arab citizens are the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homes during the 1948 Arab-Israel war at the time of Israel’s independence. Today, they mostly live in separate towns from Jewish Israelis and face violence and discriminatory housing policies. Over the decades, disagreements, including over Israel’s nature as a Jewish state, have led many Arab voters to avoid the ballot box. This week, many Arab voters said they were furious at Mr. Netanyahu for his treatment of the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and for policies that they feel treat Palestinians in Israel as second-class citizens. Indeed, throughout the campaign, Mr. Netanyahu made overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice. “I’m very optimistic because people understand that this isn’t like ordinary elections — we want change,” said Kholoud Al-Zeinati, 39, an Arab Israeli voter who cast her ballot on Tuesday in the mixed Jewish-Arab city of Lod, where long lines formed at polling places. “Because we, as the Arab community, are the community that pays the biggest price across so many aspects of life, it’s important to come out and take part.” “I expect our votes to be truly decisive in shaping the next government and making things better for all of us,” she added. Of the two Arab parties that did well on Tuesday, only Raam has joined a coalition government in the past. That happened in 2021, when it joined the short-lived anti-Netanyahu coalition of Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. Raam’s participation in that government outraged many right-wing Jewish voters, and when it collapsed after roughly one year, they backed Mr. Netanyahu, who went on to form the most hard-line government in Israel’s history. That government now faces the possibility that it may be brought down by an election result that has been deeply shaped by robust Arab turnout. Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting from Lod, Israel. The longevity of his most recent governing coalition followed three years during which a cycle of collapsed coalitions and five snap elections had left the country without a functional government or national budget. In 2021, Israelis ousted Mr. Netanyahu from power and then returned him to office 18 months later. He had staged a previous comeback, in 2009, becoming prime minister a decade after his party was voted out of power. March 2021 Ousted by a single-seat majority In 2021, Mr. Netanyahu’s government collapsed after failing to pass a budget, setting off legislative elections. At the time, he had been indicted on charges of fraud, bribery and breach of trust , and the coalition he was leading was shaky. According to analysts , heading into an election was a gambit by Mr. Netanyahu to strengthen his grip on power before his criminal trial. But the electorate that voted that March didn’t give him the seats he needed, ending a period of 12 straight years in office for him. It took months of wrangling for an eclectic coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces to cobble together a single-seat majority in the Parliament. Naftali Bennett, a right-wing former ally of Mr. Netanyahu’s, led the coalition as prime minister, hammering out a deal with Yair Lapid, a centrist and former broadcaster who was appointed foreign minister. The eight-party coalition proved too unwieldy to endure. After two right-wing lawmakers defected and several on the left rebelled in critical votes, that government collapsed in June 2022 . November 2022 Returned to office by a hard-line coalition After the resulting elections, held in November 2022, Mr. Netanyahu returned to power as right-wing voters moved to more extreme parties, diminishing the center left. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party allied with far-right and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers to secure a clear majority in the Parliament , forming the most hard-line and religious conservative government in Israel’s history. The coalition accounted for 48.4 percent of the vote but had a parliamentary majority because two anti-Netanyahu parties — one leftist, one Arab nationalist — fell just short of the share of votes needed to obtain seats. It was a reminder of how tiny swings among voters can have a big effect under Israel’s parliamentary system. Mr. Netanyahu has since overseen an acceleration of the country’s rightward shift, including an effort to overhaul the judiciary that prompted huge street protests. Questions about whether his government could have better pre-empted the Oct. 7 attack have also become hot-button issues . In April, Mr. Lapid and Mr. Bennett said they would reconstitute their centrist alliance of 2021 for the 2026 election. Mr. Netanyahu will also face Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who leads the largest opposition party . “It’s over,” he said. “It’s only a matter of time.” The comments were a reflection of Israel’s deepening global isolation, with even once-staunch allies imposing or threatening economic sanctions and embargoes after years of war in Gaza and rampant violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. With settlers advancing into areas that were previously off limits, Britain last month decried what it called “ethnic cleansing” and announced trade sanctions on settlements that it said would also apply to entities that financed their construction. Though Israel’s banking system has not been directly targeted by sanctions, a dozen countries, including Canada, France and Spain, have said they support restrictions on trade with settlements, raising the prospect of further penalties that could affect Israeli financial institutions. items.title: Fed Will Hold Fewer Rate-Setting Meetings Starting Next Year
items.summary: Kevin M. Warsh, the Federal Reserve’s chairman, said the central bank would vote on interest rates seven times in 2027 and six in 2028. It has traditionally voted eight times per year.

items.title: Takeaways from Warsh’s news conference.
items.full_text: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, despite no recent progress on getting inflation down to the central bank’s 2 percent target. Officials voted 10-2 to keep rates at the range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. That range was reached in September after policymakers decided unanimously to raise rates for the first time since 2023. Lisa D. Cook, a Fed governor who President Trump has tried to fire, issued her first-ever dissent on the Fed’s monetary policy settings in favor of a quarter-point increase on Wednesday. She was joined by Beth M. Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, who has dissented repeatedly this year. In a statement accompanying the rate decision , the Fed conveyed that it had more work to do to quell inflation, which it described as “elevated.” At a news conference after the decision, Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, started with an upbeat assessment of the economy, but stressed that inflation was still too high. He also said the central bank would cut the number of meetings at which it votes on interest rates. Mr. Warsh said the Fed would still meet eight times in 2027, but one of those meetings would focus “exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy” and would not include a vote on interest rates. Starting in 2028, the Fed plans to dedicate two meetings to such broader strategy. The Fed gathered days before midterm elections that will decide whether Republicans retain control of Congress and how much scope President Trump will have to enact his agenda in the second half of his term. Affordability issues are central for voters after nearly six years in which inflation has overshot the Fed’s target. “Politics played no role in the decision,” Mr. Warsh said when asked about the midterms. Mr. Warsh, who took over as chairman of the Fed in May, has made taming inflation the top priority of his four-year term. Since officials at the Fed met in September, inflation data has been far from reassuring. Price pressures appear to be broadening out after shocks caused by Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the U.S.-Israel war with Iran. Energy prices have shot higher, threatening to spill over into other goods and services. The economy has continued to grow at a solid pace despite these headwinds, fueled by an investment boom stemming from companies scrambling to expand their artificial intelligence capabilities. Wage gains have failed to keep up with rising prices, however, meaning Americans are earning less for an hour of work. U.S. government borrowing costs have risen sharply, making not only mortgages and other consumer loans more expensive, but also financing for companies. Certain A.I. companies, which have issued a significant amount of debt to fund their expansion plans, appear particularly exposed. As a result, financial conditions, which track the availability of credit across the economy, appear slightly less accommodative. To what extent this will help the Fed tame inflation depends in large part on whether these conditions tighten further. Ms. Hammack’s dissent on Wednesday was widely expected given her views that the Fed’s policy settings are not restraining the economy. Ms. Cook’s dissent was notable in that she is locked in a legal battle with Mr. Trump, who has sought to pressure the Fed into lowering rates. Ms. Cook became a target in the summer of 2025 when the president seized on unproven allegations that she committed mortgage fraud before joining the central bank. Mr. Trump renewed that effort after the Supreme Court ruled against him on the matter earlier this year. The White House started its own investigation into Ms. Cook and summoned her in for an in-person hearing. In a news conference on Wednesday, Mr. Warsh said the Fed would meet eight times next year as usual. But only seven of those meetings will include a vote on interest rates. The eighth “will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy,” he said. In 2028, the Fed expects to hold just six rate-setting meetings, with two meetings dedicated to discussions of longer-run strategy, Mr. Warsh said. “Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information rich intervals,” Mr. Warsh said, “but it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.” Some economists have criticized the idea of holding fewer meetings, arguing it could make it harder for the Fed to respond quickly to changes in inflation and the labor market. The move also fits a pattern during the early months of Mr. Warsh’s chairmanship toward providing less information to investors and the public, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater openness. Other economists, however, have defended the idea. They argue that providing more time between meetings will make it easier for policymakers to identify meaningful shifts in economic conditions. And they note that the Fed can hold emergency meetings if necessary, as it has done numerous times in the past.

The move also fits a pattern during the early months of Mr. Warsh’s chairmanship toward providing less information to investors and the public, reversing a decades-long trend toward greater openness. Other economists, however, have defended the idea. They argue that providing more time between meetings will make it easier for policymakers to identify meaningful shifts in economic conditions. And they note that the Fed can hold emergency meetings if necessary, as it has done numerous times in the past. Lisa D. Cook, a Fed governor whom President Trump has tried to fire, issued her first-ever dissent on the Fed’s monetary policy settings, voting in favor of a quarter-point increase. She was joined by Beth M. Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, who has dissented a number of times this year. In a statement accompanying the rate decision , the Fed conveyed that it still had more work to do to quell inflation, which it described as “elevated.” “The accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2 percent goal,” it said. That message aligned with comments from top policymakers in the lead-up to October’s meeting. Several officials signaled their support for another rate increase later this year, even as they argued that there was no urgency to deliver increases at back-to-back meetings. The central bank gathered just days before midterm elections that will decide whether Republicans will retain control of Congress and in turn, how much scope President Trump will have to enact his agenda in the second half of his term. Affordability issues are front and center for voters after nearly six years in which inflation has overshot the Fed’s target. Kevin M. Warsh, who took over as chairman of the central bank in May, told reporters that politics did not factor into the Fed’s decision on Wednesday. Instead, he suggested that the Fed had the flexibility to wait and accumulate more information before its next meeting in December. He pointed to the fact that the public does not appear to be losing confidence in the Fed’s ability to eventually achieve its 2 percent target and that there were not yet signs that the economy was overheating. “Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy too strong? That isn’t the judgment of most of my colleagues,” said Mr. Warsh. Mr. Warsh also leaned into the fact that financial conditions, which track the availability of credit across the economy, appear slightly less accommodative than they have in the past. U.S. government borrowing costs have risen sharply in recent months, making not only mortgages and other consumer loans more expensive, but also financing for companies. Certain artificial intelligence companies, which have issued a significant amount of debt to fund expansion plans, appear particularly exposed, sparking a sell-off in technology stocks as recently as last week. On Wednesday, the short-dated, two-year Treasury yield fell to 4.72 percent while the 10-year Treasury yield rose before settling around 5.02 percent. The move in the 10-year was driven by a rise in the break-even inflation rate, which is a market measure of investors’ inflation expectations. Mr. Warsh stopped short of describing financial conditions as “tight,” but he noted that “market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations.” Later in the news conference, he said this shift wasn’t something that the Fed was “uncomfortable with.” “It tells me the policy is working, and I think we can do that and make the economy more durable, have it last longer, and still achieve stable prices,” he said. The chairman was on the defensive on Wednesday because the incoming inflation data since the central bank’s last meeting has been far from reassuring. Price pressures appear to be broadening out after a series of recent shocks caused first by Mr. Trump’s tariffs and later by the U.S.-Israel war with Iran. Energy prices have shot higher across the board, threatening to spill over into other goods and services. The economy has continued to grow at a solid pace despite these headwinds, fueled in large part by an investment boom stemming from companies scrambling to expand their A.I. capabilities. Prices for computer chips and other crucial components have risen sharply, contributing to higher inflation. Wage gains have failed to keep up with rising prices, however, meaning Americans are earning less for an hour of work. Asked specifically about A.I., Mr. Warsh pushed back on the idea that the sector is insensitive to higher rates , citing recent market ructions in that space. Investors were “discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make,” he noted. Mr. Warsh also stressed the productivity gains that he expects the proliferation of this technology to continue to fuel. “Economic growth is higher, but that doesn’t tell me that economic growth is somehow causing inflation and making our job harder.” he said. Ms. Cook’s dissent was notable for two reasons. She is the first governor on the Fed’s board to vote against a policy decision since Mr. Warsh took over as chairman.
